subject: research/osrobot-dofbom
professional: a robotics hardware engineer who costs low-cost arms (SO-100/101, Koch, XLeRobot class) for build runs; first checks: do the unit prices match the cited parts list, is the power supply matched to the servo voltage, are one-off tools kept out of the per-unit BOM, are the headline ratios pinned by tests, and is the comparison like-for-like (same servo class)

evidence.correctness: Fetched the cited SO-ARM101 README (raw.githubusercontent.com/uofrobotics/SO-ARM101/main/README.md, and upstream TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100, same totals) and checked every unit price in bom.py:9-16 against the 'Parts for One Follower Arm' table (lines 93-99): servo $13.89, board $10.60, USB-C 2pcs $7, PSU $10, clamp 2pcs $5, screwdriver $6, total $121.94: all match. Two-arm table (lines 76-84): 7+2+3=12 servos x 13.89 + 2x10.6 + 7 + 2x10 + 9 + 6 = 229.88: matches. Hand: total(2)=2x13.89+38.60=66.38, total(6)=83.34+38.60=121.94, ratio 1.837; RobotShop 2j 98.44+38.60=137.04, 6j 295.32+38.60=333.92, ratio 2.437; closed form for ratio 2.5: s=38.6x1.5/(6-5)=57.90, 2.9: 38.6x1.9/0.2=366.70; printed 0.1 kg x $40 = $4.00 -> 70.38. All match the model and results.txt. Re-running experiments/run.py and figure.py left git diff empty (results reproduce byte for byte). Not a 4: the $26.00 and $49.22 rows pair the 12 V 30 kg.cm servo with the table's $10 5 V supply, while the same source (line 70) says the 12 V servo needs a 12 V 5 A+ supply instead; and the $6 screwdriver set, a one-off tool, is counted as a per-arm fixed part in every headline ratio (without it the table-servo ratio is 1.92, not 1.84).
evidence.completeness: Claims checked end to end: 8 tests (8 pass), run.py writes the five sweeps quoted in the README (all numbers in the README bullets match results.txt), figure.py regenerates bom.svg from results.txt (identical), live page https://marisstella.app/research/osrobot-dofbom/ returns 200 and carries the 1.84 headline. Every README input-table row has a source in bom.py. No stubs or TODOs. Next steps (camera, mount, stop, same-part comparison, value side) are listed as not done.
evidence.verification: `cd research/osrobot-dofbom && PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`: 8 tests OK in 0.001 s. Four seeded mutants with platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: one extra servo on every non-gripper arm (bom.py:37) SURVIVED although it moves the headline ratio from 1.84 to 1.69; servo_price_for_ratio (target-1.0)->(target-0.9) (bom.py:58) SURVIVED (the function has no test); ratio numerator +$6 (bom.py:53) SURVIVED (no test asserts any ratio value, only 1 < r < 3); dropping the PSU line (bom.py:38) was caught by the follower-total test. The two-arm test (tests/test_bom.py:12-15) evaluates a literal arithmetic expression and never calls the model, so it cannot fail.
evidence.craft: Read bom.py (58 lines), test_bom.py, run.py, figure.py. Small, pure, stdlib, each constant sourced in a comment. Defects: `from osrobot_dofbom.bom import *` in tests and run.py; the two-arm 'check' in both test_bom.py:14 and run.py:35 is a hand-typed sum, not a model call (bom() cannot express two boards / two PSUs / a 4-clamp pack); printed_kg(n) takes n and ignores it (documented); servo_price_for_ratio has no guard for target >= n_hi/n_lo (division by zero or negative price).
evidence.claims: Backed: every price (SO-ARM101 table, fetched), follower total exact (test), all README bullet numbers (results.txt), live page, AI-assistance and no-affiliation notes, limitations list. Not backed: README 'The model reproduces the table's totals: ... the two-arm set $229.88, both exact (tests/test_bom.py)': the model is never run on two arms, the test checks a literal. Framing: the title/lede 'About 1.8 times, not 3' rebuts osrobot-dof's 'triple the servo bill', which was stated for the 12 V retail servo ($26/$49.22); at those prices the full-BOM ratio is 2.15-2.44. The 1.84 comes from switching to the cheaper 7.4 V part and counting a screwdriver set as BOM. The limitation is disclosed in the README, but the headline leads with the least comparable case.
evidence.fitness: Job walked: a researcher wants the cost of 2 vs 6 joints for a feeding arm. They get (F+6s)/(F+2s) with F=$38.60, a correct one-line identity plus the cited table. Nearest prior work: the SO-ARM101/SO-ARM100 sourcing tables themselves (which already give $121.94 for the 6-servo arm), XLeRobot's published $660 dual-arm BOM in the same README, and assistive feeding arms (Obi, Kinova JACO, UW ADA) whose cost drivers (mount, camera, safety stop, compute) are exactly what is unpriced here. The result is sound but thin: the novelty is noting that fixed parts dilute a servo-only ratio, and every total is a lower bound by the README's own admission, so the 2-vs-6 ratio for a real feeding arm (with camera, mount, compute adding to F) would be lower still and is not estimated.
evidence.domain: Compared against how a hardware engineer builds a costed BOM: per-unit BOM separate from tooling/NRE (screwdrivers here are in), supply matched to actuator voltage (12 V servos rows use the 5 V supply, contrary to the source's own note), like-for-like part class across the comparison (mixed 7.4 V and 12 V), printed parts and shipping/tariff priced or bounded (filament only swept, printing time/printer not), and the mounting/compute/sensing items that dominate a feeding arm. It also does not check whether a 2-joint arm can use the same servo (hand: shoulder holding torque ~0.64 N.m = 6.5 kg.cm at 0.5 m reach, within the 7.4 V part's 16.5 kg.cm, so it can; not stated).

defects.what: Headline ratios are not pinned by any test: mutants adding a servo to every arm (ratio 1.84 -> 1.69), shifting the ratio numerator, or changing servo_price_for_ratio all survive; tests only assert 1 < ratio < 3
The $26.00 and $49.22 rows are the 12 V servo but keep the $10 5 V supply; the cited source says the 12 V servo needs a 12 V 5 A+ supply instead, so the 2.15 and 2.44 ratios use a wrong fixed part
README says the model reproduces the two-arm $229.88 total via tests/test_bom.py, but that test (and run.py:35) evaluates a hand-typed sum and never calls the model
Headline 'about 1.8 times, not 3' rebuts osrobot-dof's 12 V servo claim using the cheaper 7.4 V part; at osrobot-dof's own prices the ratio is 2.15-2.44 (disclosed only in Limitations)
A one-off screwdriver set is counted as a per-arm fixed part in every headline ratio (1.84 with it, 1.92 without)
servo_price_for_ratio has no guard for target >= n_hi/n_lo or <= 1 (division by zero / negative price)
Feeding-arm cost drivers (mount, camera, compute, safety stop) unpriced, so the 2-vs-6 ratio for a real feeding arm is not estimated even as a bound

verdict: Below the bar. The arithmetic is right and the prices are real: every unit price matches the cited SO-ARM101 table, the follower ($121.94) and two-arm ($229.88) totals match the source, and five hand recomputations (66.38, 121.94, ratio 1.837, RobotShop 2.437, break-even servo $57.90/$366.70) agree; results and figure reproduce byte for byte. But the tests pin only the follower total: three of four seeded mutants in core logic, including one that moves the headline ratio from 1.84 to 1.69, survive; the README's 'two-arm total reproduced by the model' is a literal sum in the test; the 12 V servo rows keep a 5 V supply the source says must be replaced; and the headline 'about 1.8, not 3' rebuts a 12 V servo claim using the 7.4 V part plus a screwdriver set. Verification, claims, fitness and domain are 2, so the bar fails on the verification and claims gates and the median.
